reasons: Cognate verb is secure: ON rjóða = Gk ἐρεύθω < *h1réudh-e- (Kroonen: 'identical to Gr. ἐρεύθω'; OE rēodan 'stain with blood'). Texts verified: Rígsþula 37 in AM 242 fol (Codex Wormianus) reads 'vǫll nam at rioða' (transmitted, menota diplomatic/normalised); Reginsmál 26 'sás fold ryði'. Greek: Il. 11.394 αἵματι γαῖαν ἐρεύθων, Il. 18.329 γαῖαν ἐρεῦσαι. But the earth noun is renewed (vǫllr/fold vs γαῖα), the image is natural battle language, and the semantic role differs: in Greek the subject reddening the earth is the dying man with his own blood (11.394 is the victim of Diomedes' missile, not 'a slain man's killer' as the lead says; 18.329 Achilles and Patroclus are to die there), whereas in Norse the killer reddens the field. Il. 10.484 uses a different, intransitive derivative ἐρυθαίνετο with γαῖα as subject. One cognate element in a partly congruent frame.

reasons: Anchor is Norwegian/Icelandic law prose (AM 56 4to, Landslǫg type): a witness who 'hæfír seet eða hǫyrt' must testify. Greek: Hermes' denial 'οὐκ ἴδον οὐ πυθόμην οὐκ ἄλλου μῦθον ἄκουσα' (H.Herm. 263 = 363). reasons: Anchor: Þiðreks saga (Holm perg 4 fol) 'hans nafn mun aldrigi tynaz i þyðværskri tungo' of the dead Sigurðr. nafn ~ ὄνομα (*h1nómn̥) cognate, but the predicate is non-cognate and the 'name never forgotten' topos is universal. Þiðreks saga is translation literature from Low German sources with courtly vocabulary (kurtæisi), so derivative risk is high. Theognis 245-246 is a fair parallel (ἄφθιτον ... ὄνομα, beside κλέος), but Pindar O. 6.57 'ὄνυμ' ἀθάνατον' is the naming of the infant Iamos for all time, not posthumous fame: wrong context.

reasons: Anchor is a late lyric ballad of the Vanka-the-Keyholder type (Kireevskij), describing the handsome youth: 'Его ясныя очи огнемъ горятъ', later contrasted with 'очи заплаканы'; it is beauty/vigour, not rage. Homer Il. 12.466 (Hector, πυρὶ δ' ὄσσε δεδήει) and 1.104 (Agamemnon's anger, ὄσσε ... πυρὶ λαμπετόωντι ἐΐκτην) are anger. Only the eye noun is cognate (очи ~ ὄσσε < *h3okw-); fire nouns and verbs renewed; 'eyes burn with fire' is a universal metaphor.

reasons: Anchor: Kirsha Danilov-type bylina (Mikhailo Kazarinov), 'И тур рогъ меду сладкаго' (line 6281 transmitted; note line 6278 '[Меду сладкаго]' is an editorial bracket supplement). The partner witnesses carry both cognates: Od. 9.162 (= 10.184, 12.30) μέθυ ἡδύ in the feasting line; Finn. 39 swētne medo (hall-drink repaid in battle); RV 1.187.2a svā́do pito mádho pito; AVŚ 18.1.95 svāduṣ kila ayam madhumāṁ (verified at that locus in the index numbering; = RV 6.47.1); AVP 19.29.22 svādoś cin ... madhoś cin. This Gk-Ved-OE noun-epithet pair is cognate on both elements in drink/feast contexts, but 'sweet honey/mead' is the most natural epithet possible, so inheritance cannot be separated from independent formation.

reasons: Völuspá (GKS 2365 4to, 2r:28) 'Munu ósánir akrar vaxa' is the transmitted text; Od. 9.109-111 ἄσπαρτα καὶ ἀνήροτα πάντα φύονται ... Διὸς ὄμβρος ἀέξει. vaxa ~ ἀέξω (*h2weg-s-) is cognate, but in Greek the intransitive slot is held by non-cognate φύονται and ἀέξει is transitive with rain as subject; 'unsown' adjectives are equivalent, not cognate. The self-growing-crops golden-age motif is also classical/learned (Hesiod Erga 117-118, Vergil Ecl. 4, Ovid Met. 1.109) and Völuspá's renewal stanza is suspected of Christian/sibylline influence. Motif parallel at best, no shared wording.
known: Völuspá's unsown fields have been compared with classical golden-age/sibylline imagery.

reasons: Anchor: Egill's lausavísa (Wolf-Aug 9 10 4to 47r:26) 'Berg-Ǫnund benjum bensvǽfðan'. The sleep part is svæfa < *swebjan-, which Kroonen calls a late causative to *sufan- 'lull to sleep, calm', root *swep- fine. But the lead's claim that ben/benjum continues *gwhen- is wrong: Kroonen derives *banjō- 'wound' (and bani) from *bhon-, explicitly rejecting *gwh > b. So there is no cognate killing element with Skt hato/nihato. The Serbian witness (Vuk 28305:39 'мртви сан заспао') is literal deep sleep: the hero is asleep and is then bound and captured, not killed. Il. 11.241 χάλκεον ὕπνον and MBh 3.154.57 / 9.30.73 (hato ... svapsyasi, nihato bhūmau svapsyasi) are genuine death-as-sleep, but death-as-sleep is universal and the formulations are all different.
known: Death as sleep, including Homeric χάλκεος ὕπνος, is a commonplace in the literature (sleep and death as brothers).

reasons: Anchor (skaldic verse in Óláfs saga/Heimskringla, AM 36 fol 424:29): 'bloð com varmt i víðan ... ægi', warm blood running into the sea. Il. 11.266: Agamemnon fights 'while the blood still welled warm (αἷμ' ἔτι θερμόν) from the wound'. varmr ~ θερμός (*gwhor-mo-/*gwher-mo-, accepted by Kroonen) is a genuine cognate, but blood is literally warm, the noun is renewed, predicates differ, and the contexts differ (slaughter at sea vs one's own wound). Generic.

Same figure as L002 (rjóða = ἐρεύθω < *h1reudh-, earth and blood nouns renewed), and the same evidence (Il. 11.394, 18.329, Rígsþula 37) plus Egill's 'rjóðum sverð í blóði' (51v:19). The slab anchor itself (Wolf-Aug 38v:1, Egill's rune verse 'rjóðum spjǫll í dreyra') reddens carved runes with blood, a magic act, not ground in a killing, so it does not show the figure; Egill 51v:19 reddens a sword, the usual ON object. The Greek role difference noted under L002 (the dying man reddens the earth) also applies. Weak at most, and only through the L002 evidence.

reasons: Anchor: Russian lyric song (Kireevskij), 'Сушитъ-то—крушить меня, молодца, печаль-горе' (grief dries me up). Etymology fine: Ru. сушить < *sušiti, which LIV (via Derksen) equates with Skt śoṣáyati < *h2sous-eie-; Skt śuṣyati is the intransitive of the same root. Rām. Su. 34.55 (śuṣyati śoka-dīnam, of Rāma's face withering like a lotus) and 17.14 (Sītā śuṣyantīm ... śoka-parāyaṇām) show grief-wasting with the same root. But one element only (sorrow nouns renewed), causative vs intransitive, late Russian folksong, and 'grief withers/dries' is a natural metaphor also found in the Psalms (derivative risk via Church Slavonic).
